content: There is no available data on the use of this therapy in pregnant women to assess the risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. Based on animal reproduction studies, telavancin may cause harm to the fetus. Pregnant women should be informed of the potential risks to the fetus. The background risk of major birth defects and miscarriage in the indicated population is unknown. In studies involving rats, rabbits, and minipigs, telavancin administered intravenously during organogenesis at doses approximately 1-2 times the maximum recommended human dose was associated with limb and skeletal malformations. Pregnancy status should be verified in females of reproductive potential before initiating therapy. There is no data on the presence of telavancin in human breast milk, its effects on a breastfed child, or its impact on milk production. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for telavancin and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed child from the drug or the underlying maternal condition. Telavancin is an antibiotic used to treat serious bacterial infections of the skin and certain types of pneumonia. It is administered via intravenous injection, typically once daily, and should be infused slowly over 60 minutes. Patients administering this medication at home should be thoroughly instructed by a healthcare professional on preparation and usage. The product should be visually inspected for particles or discoloration before use, and any compromised product should not be used. Infusion reactions, such as flushing of the upper body, may occur if the drug is infused too quickly. Patients should report any symptoms of infusion reactions to their doctor immediately. For optimal effectiveness, telavancin should be used at evenly spaced intervals, and the full prescribed course should be completed, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Common side effects may include a metallic or soapy taste, nausea, vomiting, or foamy urine. Rarely, this medication may cause a severe intestinal condition due to Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile), which can occur during treatment or weeks to months after treatment has stopped. Prolonged or repeated use may lead to oral thrush or new vaginal yeast infections. Serious allergic reactions are rare but possible. Kidney function tests should be performed before, during, and after treatment to monitor for potential kidney issues. Patients with moderate to severe kidney disease using telavancin to treat serious lung infections may be at an increased risk of death. Women of childbearing age should use reliable forms of birth control while taking telavancin and for two days after the last dose, as the medication may harm an unborn baby. A pregnancy test may be required before starting treatment. During pregnancy, telavancin should only be used when clearly necessary, and its potential risks should be discussed with a healthcare provider. It is unknown if telavancin passes into breast milk. Telavancin may affect heart rhythm (QT prolongation), and the risk may be higher in individuals with certain medical conditions, low potassium or magnesium levels, or those taking medications that also prolong the QT interval. It may also interfere with live bacterial vaccines (e.g., typhoid vaccine) and certain lab tests, potentially causing false results. Patients should inform their doctor or pharmacist of any allergies or other medications they are taking to avoid potential drug interactions. In the event of an overdose, seek emergency medical attention immediately. Proper storage and disposal of the medication should follow the product instructions or pharmacist guidance. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about telavancin. Patients should consult their healthcare provider for complete information tailored to their specific health needs.
